title: Up Reisen gohn
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 143. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 143's title is Low German for "going traveling," and the tale is a chain of a young man's misfortune, entirely in dialect: sent out with nothing but a phrase to repeat, he is beaten for saying the wrong stock line to fishermen, then to a hangman's crowd, then to a knacker, then to a cartful of people, because each new phrase he's given fits the last situation, not the next one. It is a comic tale of bad timing, and it ends exactly where its title promises, with the boy done traveling for good.

sentences.t: Et was emol ne arme Frau, de hadde enen Suhn, de wull so gerne reisen,
sentences.l: There was once a poor woman, she had a son, who wanted so gladly to travel,
sentences.i: There was once a poor woman who had a son, and the son wanted so much to go travelling,
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), Westphalian. Et = es; was here is war, “was” — the dialect word for “what” is wat; emol = einmal; ne = eine; de = der/die, here “who”; hadde = hatte; Suhn = Sohn; wull = wollte. “Up Reisen gohn,” the title, is auf Reisen gehen — to go out on the road.

sentences.t: do seg de Mohr „wu kannst du reisen? wi hebt je gar kien Geld, dat du mitniemen kannst.“
sentences.l: then said the mother “how can you travel? we have no money at all, that you could take with you.”
sentences.i: Then the mother said: “How can you go travelling? We have no money at all for you to take with you.”
sentences.n: Mohr is the Westphalian word for Mutter, the mother — it has nothing to do with the High German word it looks like. Two more forms to hold on to, because they run through every second line: seg is sagte, “said” (seggen = sagen, not sehen), and hebt is haben, “we have” (hebben) — not heben, “to lift.” wu = wie; je is the particle ja, expecting agreement; kien = kein; mitniemen = mitnehmen, with mit- in front and the verb at the end.

sentences.t: Do seg de Suhn „ick will mi gut behelpen, ick will alltied seggen „nig viel, nig viel, nig viel.“
sentences.l: Then said the son “I will make do for myself well, I will always say ‘not much, not much, not much.’”
sentences.i: Then the son said: “I shall get along well enough; I shall always say: ‘Not much, not much, not much.’”
sentences.n: “sich behelpen” = sich behelfen, to make do, to get by on what one has. alltied = allezeit, always. The boy’s whole plan is one phrase for every occasion, and the tale is what happens when one phrase meets a world that keeps changing. The 1857 text opens the inner quotation and never closes it — the same happens at each of the three instructions that follow.

sentences.t: Do genk he ene gude Tied un sede alltied „nig viel, nig viel, nig viel.“
sentences.l: Then went he a good while and said always “not much, not much, not much.”
sentences.i: Then he walked a good long while, saying all the time: “Not much, not much, not much.”
sentences.n: genk = ging; “ene gude Tied” = eine gute Zeit, a good while; sede = sagte. The tale slides between past and present from sentence to sentence — genk, then kümmt, then geit — as a spoken telling does; English cannot follow that without sounding careless, so the idiomatic line keeps to the past.

sentences.t: Kam do bi en Trop Fisker un seg „Gott helpe ju! nig viel, nig viel, nig viel.“
sentences.l: Came then upon a troop of fishermen and said “God help you! not much, not much, not much.”
sentences.i: Then he came upon a party of fishermen and said: “God help you! Not much, not much, not much.”
sentences.n: The sentence starts straight in with its verb and no subject — “Kam do” — a way of hurrying on in a told story. Trop = Trupp, a party; bi = bei; “Gott helpe ju” = Gott helfe euch, the ordinary greeting called to men at work, like “God speed.” He hangs his phrase on the end of a blessing, and it lands on the catch.

sentences.t: „Wat segst du, Kerl, nig viel?“
sentences.l: “What say you, fellow, ‘not much’?”
sentences.i: “What are you saying, fellow — ‘not much’?”
sentences.n: segst = sagst. Kerl is a rough form of address, not a friendly one. The same challenge comes back almost word for word at each of the disasters to follow.

sentences.t: Un asse dat Gören (Garn) uttrocken, kregen se auck nig viel Fiske.
sentences.l: And as [they] drew the Gören (net) out, they got also not much fish.
sentences.i: And when they drew out the net, sure enough they took not much fish.
sentences.n: (Garn) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis, printed in the 1857 text to explain the dialect Gören to their own readers; the literal line keeps the dialect word and puts their gloss, translated, in the brackets. Gören = Garn, the net; uttrocken = auszogen (uttrecken = ausziehen, to haul out) — its subject is left out, so I have supplied [they] in square brackets. auck = auch, here “sure enough, just as he said.” Fiske = Fische. His phrase has worked like a spell.

sentences.t: So met enen Stock up de Jungen, un „hest du mi nig dresken (dreschen) seihn?“
sentences.l: So [they went] with a stick at the boy, and “have you not seen me dresken (thresh)?”
sentences.i: So they went at the boy with a stick: “Have you not seen me threshing?”
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb at all — “So met enen Stock up de Jungen” is the whole of it, the way a teller acts a thing out instead of saying it; I have supplied [they went] in square brackets so the English can stand. (dreschen) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis for the dialect dresken. What the fisherman means is arguable: either “did you not see what work I was at?” or, with the stick already in his hand, “have you not felt me thresh you?” seihn = gesehen; de Jungen is the boy (the noun), not the adjective jung.

sentences.t: „Wat sall ick denn seggen?“ seg de Junge.
sentences.l: “What shall I then say?” said the boy.
sentences.i: “What should I say, then?” said the boy.
sentences.n: denn here is the little question-word — was soll ich denn sagen? — not denn “for, because.” sall = soll. This exchange, question and instruction, returns at each beating with barely a word changed.

sentences.t: „Du sallst seggen „fank vull, fank vull.“
sentences.l: “You shall say ‘catch full, catch full.’”
sentences.i: “You are to say: ‘A full catch, a full catch.’”
sentences.n: sallst = sollst. “fank vull” = fang voll — the fisherman’s own blessing, exactly what he wanted said over his nets, and exactly the wrong thing to say anywhere else.

sentences.t: Do geit he wier ene ganze Tied un seg „fank vull, fank vull,“
sentences.l: Then goes he again a whole while and says “catch full, catch full,”
sentences.i: Then he went on again a good while, saying “A full catch, a full catch,”
sentences.n: geit = geht — the present tense again; wier = wieder. The shape repeats: he walks, he says yesterday’s phrase, and today is not yesterday.

sentences.t: bis he kümmt an enen Galgen, do hebt se en armen Sünder, den willt se richten.
sentences.l: until he comes to a gallows, there have they a poor sinner, whom they want to execute.
sentences.i: until he came to a gallows, where they had a poor sinner whom they meant to put to death.
sentences.n: hebt is haben, “they have” — the same form as the mother’s “wi hebt” in the opening line, not heben, “to lift.” willt = wollen (plural). richten here is to execute, to carry out a sentence, not richten “to direct.” “Ein armer Sünder” is the set phrase for a condemned man on his way to the gallows — poor in the sense of pitiable, and the crowd is there to pray for him.

sentences.t: Do seg he „guden Morgen, fank vull, fank vull.“
sentences.l: Then said he “good morning, catch full, catch full.”
sentences.i: Then he said: “Good morning — a full catch, a full catch.”
sentences.n: guden Morgen = guten Morgen. He has added a greeting and kept yesterday’s blessing, and so wishes the hangmen a good haul.

sentences.t: „Wat segst du, Kerl, fank vull? söllt der noch mehr leige (leidige, böse) Lude in de Welt sien? is düt noch nig genog?“
sentences.l: “What say you, fellow, ‘catch full’? should there still more leige (odious, wicked) people in the world be? is this not yet enough?”
sentences.i: “What are you saying, fellow — ‘a full catch’? Are there to be still more wicked people in the world? Is this not enough?”
sentences.n: (leidige, böse) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis, printed in the text to explain the dialect leige. der here is da, “there” — the expletive of “sollten da noch mehr … sein?” — and not the article; Lude = Leute; düt = dies; genog = genug. The hangman hears the phrase as a wish for more men to hang.

sentences.t: He krig wier wat up den Puckel.
sentences.l: He got again something upon the back.
sentences.i: He got another beating across his back.
sentences.n: krig = kriegte; Puckel is the Buckel, the hump of the back — “wat up den Puckel kriegen,” to get something across the back, is still a living German phrase for a thrashing. wier = wieder: this is the second of three.

sentences.t: „Wat sall ik denn seggen?“
sentences.l: “What shall I then say?”
sentences.i: “What should I say, then?”
sentences.n: Spelled ik here and ick a few lines earlier — the 1857 text does not regularise its dialect spellings — and this time the speech tag is dropped altogether.

sentences.t: „Du sallst seggen „Gott tröst de arme Seele.“
sentences.l: “You shall say ‘God comfort the poor soul.’”
sentences.i: “You are to say: ‘God comfort the poor soul.’”
sentences.n: tröst = tröste, the wish-form: may God comfort. It is what the crowd says at an execution — and it is what will be exactly wrong at the next stop.

sentences.t: De Junge geit wier ene ganze Tied un seg „Gott tröst de arme Seele!“
sentences.l: The boy goes again a whole while and says “God comfort the poor soul!”
sentences.i: The boy went on again a good long while, saying: “God comfort the poor soul!”
sentences.n: de Junge here is the noun, the boy. The third round opens exactly like the two before it.

sentences.t: Do kümmet he an en Grawen, do steit en Filler (Schinder), de tüt en Perd af.
sentences.l: Then comes he to a ditch, there stands a Filler (knacker), who draws a horse’s hide off.
sentences.i: Then he came to a ditch, and there stood a flayer, pulling the hide off a horse.
sentences.n: Grawen here is Graben, a ditch. (Schinder) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis for the dialect Filler — the knacker, who killed and skinned worn-out beasts; his was a dishonourable trade, and those who followed it were shunned. “de tüt en Perd af” = der zieht ein Pferd ab, draws the hide off it. steit = steht; Perd = Pferd.

sentences.t: De Junge seg „guden Morgen, Gott tröst de arme Seele!“
sentences.l: The boy said “good morning, God comfort the poor soul!”
sentences.i: The boy said: “Good morning — God comfort the poor soul!”
sentences.n: Said over a dead horse being skinned, a prayer for a departing soul is an insult to the knacker and nonsense besides: the same mistake, the third time.

sentences.t: „Wat segst du, leige Kerl?“ un schleit en met sinen Filhacken üm de Ohren, dat he ut den Augen nig seihen kann.
sentences.l: “What say you, wretched fellow?” and strikes him with his flaying-hook about the ears, so that he out of his eyes cannot see.
sentences.i: “What are you saying, you wretched fellow?” — and he struck him about the ears with his flaying-hook, until he could not see out of his eyes.
sentences.n: leige = leidige, wretched — the word the Grimms glossed a few lines above. schleit = schlägt; en = ihn; a Filhacken is the knacker’s hide-hook; üm de Ohren = um die Ohren. “dat he ut den Augen nig seihen kann” = daß er aus den Augen nicht sehen kann — beaten about the head until his eyes are shut. The tale does not soften it: three working men in a row thrash the boy.

sentences.t: „Wu sall ick denn seggen?“
sentences.l: “How shall I then say?”
sentences.i: “What should I say, then?”
sentences.n: wu = wie, “how,” where the two earlier askings had wat, “what” — the dialect will use either for this question.

sentences.t: „Du sallst seggen „do ligge du Aas in en Grawen.“
sentences.l: “You shall say ‘there lie you carrion in a ditch.’”
sentences.i: “You are to say: ‘Lie there, you carcass, in a ditch.’”
sentences.n: do = da; ligge is the imperative, lieg. Aas is carrion, a dead beast — and thrown at a person it is the coarsest insult the language has. These are the knacker’s own words over the horse, which the boy will now carry to the next people he meets.

sentences.t: Do geit he un seg alltied „do ligge du Aas in en Grawen! do ligge du Aas in en Grawen!“
sentences.l: Then goes he and says always “there lie you carrion in a ditch! there lie you carrion in a ditch!”
sentences.i: Then on he went, saying all the time: “Lie there, you carcass, in a ditch! Lie there, you carcass, in a ditch!”
sentences.n: The fourth round, and by now the shape is plain: whatever he was given last is exactly what will not do next.

sentences.t: Nu kümmt he bi enen Wagen vull Lüde, do seg he „guden Morgen, do ligge du Aas in en Grawen!“
sentences.l: Now comes he upon a wagon full of people, then says he “good morning, there lie you carrion in a ditch!”
sentences.i: Now he came upon a wagon full of people, and said: “Good morning — lie there, you carcass, in a ditch!”
sentences.n: Lüde = Leute, spelled Lude a few lines earlier; vull = voll. He has wished a ditch on a wagon-load of the living.

sentences.t: Do föllt de Wagen üm in en Grawen, de Knecht kreg de Pietske un knapt den Jungen, dat he wier to sine Mohr krupen moste.
sentences.l: Then falls the wagon over into a ditch, the farmhand got the whip and thrashed the boy, so that he had to crawl back to his mother.
sentences.i: And the wagon fell over into a ditch, and the farmhand took the whip and laid into the boy, so that he had to crawl home to his mother.
sentences.n: föllt … üm = fällt um, falls over, with the prefix üm at the end — this üm is “over,” where the üm of “üm de Ohren” was “about.” Pietske = Peitsche; knapt is to snap or crack a whip at someone, here to give a hiding; krupen = kriechen; moste = mußte. His words work as a spell for the fourth time, and for the fourth time the beating is his.

sentences.t: Un he is sien Lewen nig wier up reisen gohn.
sentences.l: And he is in all his life not again gone out travelling.
sentences.i: And he never went out travelling again as long as he lived.
sentences.n: “sien Lewen” = sein Leben, an accusative of duration: all his life long. “up reisen gohn” = auf Reisen gehen, the tale’s own title, brought back to close it. The joke ends without a moral, unless it is that a phrase learnt for yesterday is worth nothing today.

glossary.denn: denn — then, in that case (the question particle: ‘wat sall ick denn seggen?’ = was soll ich denn sagen?)
glossary.der: Low German: da — there (‘söllt der noch mehr Lude sien’ = sollten da noch mehr Leute sein; the article is de)
glossary.en: Low German: ein/einen — a, an, one; but in “schleit en met sinen Filhacken” it is ihn, him
glossary.grawen: Low German: der Graben — ditch (‘in en Grawen’ = in einen Graben); not Grafen, counts
glossary.hebt: Low German: haben — have (hebben, 1st/3rd pl.; ‘wi hebt’ = wir haben)
glossary.je: Low German: ja — (particle) indeed, after all (‘wi hebt je gar kien Geld’ = wir haben ja gar kein Geld)
glossary.junge: der Junge — the boy (noun; not the adjective jung)
glossary.jungen: der Junge — the boy (acc./dat. sg. Jungen; not the adjective jung)
glossary.richten: richten — to put to death, execute (hinrichten; ‘den willt se richten’ = den wollen sie hinrichten)
glossary.seg: Low German: sagte, sagt — said, says (seggen = sagen; ‘do seg de Mohr’ = da sagte die Mutter)
glossary.was: Low German: war — was (sein, 3rd sg. past; ‘et was emol’ = es war einmal)
glossary.willt: Low German: wollen — want, mean to (3rd pl.; ‘den willt se richten’ = den wollen sie richten)
glossary.üm: Low German: um — around, about (“üm de Ohren” = um die Ohren); also the separated prefix of ümfallen (umfallen), to fall over (“föllt … üm”)
